verdict.rationale: The canon supplies one return-vocabulary, parousia, apokalypsis, and epiphaneia, all bound to a single visible bodily coming with loud trumpet, descent on clouds, and gathering of the elect (Matt 24:29-31, 1 Thess 4:16-17, 2 Thess 2:1, 1 Cor 15:52, Titus 2:13). On this footing posttrib has strong unitary lexical evidence and meta in Matt 24:29 is explicit. But three lexical realities prevent closure. First, harpazo (G0726) attests both a sudden divine removal sense (Acts 8:39, 2 Cor 12:2, Rev 12:5) and a forcible seizure sense (John 10:12, Matt 11:12), and 1 Thess 4:17 carries no temporal marker fixing the snatching relative to thlipsis. Second, tereo plus ek in Rev 3:10 lexically matches the same construction in John 17:15 where ek means kept while in, not removed from, so the preposition does not adjudicate. Third, ekklesia (G1577) is dense in Rev 1 to 3 and reappears only at 22:16, leaving Rev 4 to 19 silent on the term, which one lens reads as a removal and another as a shift in referent. The pattern is materially contested.

scripture.force: The phrase Eutheos meta ten thlipsin ton hemeron ekeinon, immediately after the tribulation of those days, places the cosmic darkening and the following appearing of the Son of Man on an explicit timeline after the thlipsis. The temporal preposition meta with the accusative articular noun is unambiguously sequential and is the load-bearing term for the posttrib reading.

The Son of Man comes erchomenon epi ton nephelon tou ouranou with power and great glory, and pasai hai phylai tes ges, all the tribes of the earth, see Him. This is overt and public, audible and visual language, not secret. The nephele plus erchomai pairing matches Dan 7:13 LXX vocabulary.

He sends His angels with a great trumpet, meta salpingos megales, and they gather the elect, episynaxousin tous eklektous autou, from the four winds, ap akron ouranon. The salpinx plus elect-gathering vocabulary overlaps directly with 1 Thess 4:16-17 (salpinx, the dead in Christ, the living caught up), supporting one event.

The Lord Himself descends from heaven en keleusmati, en phone archangelou, en salpingi theou. Every element, command shout, archangel voice, trumpet of God, is loud and audible. The vocabulary names a public theophany, not a hidden removal, and the salpinx aligns with Matt 24:31 and 1 Cor 15:52.

Hoi zontes hoi perileipomenoi, the surviving living, are harpagesometha (future passive of harpazo) together with the risen sleepers en nephelais eis apantesin tou kyriou eis aera. Harpazo across its 14 canon attestations means a sudden seizing, used for both divine removal (Acts 8:39, 2 Cor 12:2-4, Rev 12:5) and forcible human action (John 10:12, Matt 11:12, Matt 13:19). The verb itself carries no temporal marker fixing the snatching before, during, or after the thlipsis, so by lexicon alone the sequencing question is undetermined.

Paul binds the parousia of the Lord and our episynagoge ep auton, gathering to Him, under one preposition hyper and one article, the cognate noun to episynaxousin in Matt 24:31. The grammar treats the coming and the gathering as one subject, weighing against a chronological gap between them.

Ean me elthe he apostasia proton kai apokalyphthe ho anthropos tes anomias, unless the apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed. The adverb proton orders the apostasy and revealing before the Day of the Lord. The Thessalonians evidently could be shaken thinking the Day had come, which presupposes they expected to still be present for events tied to it, complicating any framework that removes the church before these signs.

Mysterion lego, pantes ou koimethesometha, pantes de allagesometha, we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. The allasso plus koimaomai pair matches 1 Thess 4 (dead in Christ rise, living caught up) and is dated en te eschate salpingi, at the last trumpet. The wording locates the change at the last salpinx, the same lexeme as Matt 24:31 and 1 Thess 4:16.

En atomo, en rhipe ophthalmou, en te eschate salpingi. The phrase eschate salpinx, last trumpet, is a definite ordinal that places the change at the final trumpet of a known series. Posttrib reads this as the same trumpet as Matt 24:31; pretrib treats it as a different last trumpet of a separate church-age sequence. The lexicon supplies one salpinx vocabulary that does not differentiate which series is in view.

Tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou, I will keep you ek of the hour of trial. The construction tereo plus ek occurs in only one other place in the canon, John 17:15, where Jesus prays the opposite of removal, hina teres autous ek tou ponerou, keep them ek of the evil one, in a context that explicitly disclaims taking them out of the world (ouk... aras autous ek tou kosmou). The same lexical construction in the canon means kept while in, not extracted from, in its only parallel. The preposition ek lexically allows both senses, motion-from and separation-from-within, and context here is contested.

John sees the psychai ton pepelekismenon dia ten martyrian Iesou kai dia ton logon tou theou, the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and the word of God, and hoitines ou prosekynesan to therion, those who did not worship the beast. Pelekizo is a canon hapax. Lexically, these are saints who refused the beast and his mark, which requires them to have been on earth during the beast and his mark era. They then live and reign with Christ.

Ouk eroto hina ares autous ek tou kosmou, all hina teres autous ek tou ponerou, I do not ask that you take them out of the world but that you keep them ek of the evil one. The verse uses the same tereo plus ek construction as Rev 3:10 and explicitly contrasts removal (airo ek) with preservation (tereo ek). It is the canon's controlling parallel for the construction and shows that ek does not entail spatial extraction.

Anesin meth hemon en te apokalypsei tou kyriou Iesou ap ouranou met angelon dynameos autou. Paul promises the thlibomenoi, the ones currently being afflicted, their relief AT (en) the apokalypsis of the Lord from heaven with the angels of His power, not before it. The temporal en links rest for the afflicted directly to the public apokalypsis, the same vocabulary used elsewhere for the visible return.

Prosdechomenoi ten makarian elpida kai epiphaneian tes doxes tou megalou theou kai soteros hemon Iesou Christou. The blessed hope is named as one event, the epiphaneia tes doxes, the manifestation of the glory, joining hope and glorious appearing under one article. Lexically the epiphaneia vocabulary always denotes visible manifestation, not a hidden phase.

En te parousia tou kyriou hemon Iesou Christou. Paul uses parousia again to date sanctification's completion, alongside its prior uses in 1 Thess 2:19, 3:13, 4:15. Across all four chapters parousia is a single referent, never differentiated into phases, so the vocabulary does not itself encode a two-stage coming.

complicating_texts.resolution: Harpagesometha asserts a sudden catching up but is temporally silent. The verb is polysemous in the canon, covering both divine rescue (Acts 8:39, 2 Cor 12:2-4, Rev 12:5) and forcible seizure (John 10:12, Matt 11:12), and 1 Thess 4:17 supplies no temporal adverb relative to the thlipsis. A separate prior removal reads the snatching as a distinct earlier event, a unitary reading folds it into the visible appearing. The lemma alone cannot adjudicate; the question remains lexically unresolved at the level of the word.

Tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou is the strongest single verse for a prior removal in the pretrib reading, but the construction tereo plus ek occurs identically in John 17:15 where it explicitly denotes preservation while in, not removal from. The preposition ek lexically allows both motion-from and separation-within senses. Because both constructions are attested with the same verb in the canon, the verse does not settle the timing question by lexicon alone.

The proton ordering of apostasy and revealing of the man of lawlessness before the Day of the Lord weighs against the church being removed before those events, but it speaks of the Day of the Lord rather than naming the gathering directly, so it informs without closing the question by itself.

Saints beheaded for refusing the beast and his mark must lexically have been on earth during the beast and mark era, supplying canon evidence that some believers go through the tribulation. A pretrib reading distinguishes these as post-rapture converts under a separate program, which is a framework distinction, not a lexical one in the verse itself.

Ekklesia (G1577) occurs 20 times in Revelation, dense in chapters 1 to 3 (the seven letters) and once at 22:16, with zero occurrences in chapters 4 to 19. One lens reads this silence as the church being removed; another reads the term as locally tied to the seven local letters and notes that hagioi, eklektoi, and doulos vocabulary continues throughout. The lexicon supplies the distribution fact but does not rank these two inferences.

variants.note: The cited passages lie in Matthew and the Thessalonian epistles, outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM was not consulted. No variant unit in the bundle bears on the timing question. The minor variants visible in Matt 24:30-31 (article on salpingos, ordering of angels) do not affect the gathering vocabulary or the meta in 24:29.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the meta ten thlipsin of Matt 24:29 as fixing the appearing after the tribulation, and the shared salpinx, nephele, episynagoge, parousia, and gathering of the elect vocabulary across Matt 24:30-31, 1 Cor 15:51-52, 1 Thess 4:16-17, 2 Thess 2:1, and 2 Thess 1:7 as describing one event. The canon's single return-vocabulary (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia), always tied to visible coming and elect-gathering, gives unitary footing without need to posit a second prior phase. 2 Thess 1:7 promises relief to the afflicted en the apokalypsis, not before it.

Reads harpagesometha in 1 Thess 4:17 as a distinct catching up of the church prior to the thlipsis, citing the temporal silence of the verb itself and the precedent uses of harpazo for sudden rescue (Acts 8:39, 2 Cor 12:2-4, Rev 12:5). Anchors a prior-removal promise in Rev 3:10 tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou and reads the absence of ekklesia in Rev 4 to 19 as the church not present during those chapters' events. Distinguishes the eschate salpinx of 1 Cor 15:52 (church-age last trumpet) from the trumpet of Matt 24:31 (a separate Israel-program trumpet).

Reads the gathering as occurring during the latter part of the seven-year period, after the apostasy and revealing of 2 Thess 2:3 but before the climactic outpouring of divine wrath. Accepts the shared parousia and salpinx vocabulary as describing one harpazo event while distinguishing the thlipsis (which the church endures) from the orge (which the church is kept from, 1 Thess 5:9). The lexicon permits this middle reading because thlipsis and orge are different lemmas with distinct distributions.

Treats the parousia, the resurrection, the judgment, and the eternal state as one consummating event with no millennial gap, and reads the gathering of 1 Thess 4 and Matt 24 as one moment at the visible return. Agrees with posttrib on the unitary lexical pattern of return-vocabulary and on Matt 24:29 meta, while differing on the millennium question.

hermeneutics.notes: The competing readings turn on how harpazo, parousia, episynagoge, thlipsis, orge, and tereo ek relate as a system, not on any disputed lexeme. The vocabulary is agreed, the sequencing model is not. The lexical pattern leans toward a unitary coming, but the verb harpazo and the tereo ek construction supply genuine room for the two-stage reading.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The gathering of believers to Christ in 1 Thess 4:16-17 occurs at, and is identical with, the visible return of Christ after the tribulation of Matt 24:29, rather than a separate prior event.
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds a verdict by asserting there is no separate prior secret rapture. The phrase secret rapture is itself a framework characterization, since 1 Thess 4:16 describes a loud command, voice, and trumpet, not secrecy, so even pretrib advocates do not describe their position as secret in that sense. The neutralized form asks the timing and unity question without presupposing the answer. The verdict below is derived on the original stem as supplied.

lay_summary: Three anchor passages supply the vocabulary. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 the Lord descends from heaven with a loud command, an archangel's voice, and the trumpet of God; the dead in Christ rise first, and the living are caught up, harpagesometha, in clouds to meet Him in the air. In Matthew 24:29-31 the Son of Man appears immediately after the tribulation, meta ten thlipsin, on the clouds with a great trumpet, and His angels gather the elect from the four winds. In 2 Thessalonians 2:1 Paul binds the coming, parousia, directly to our gathering to Him, episynagoge, the noun cognate to the gathering verb in Matthew. The same trumpet word also appears at 1 Corinthians 15:52, where the change of the living is dated at the last trumpet. Across the canon the return is named by three nouns, parousia, apokalypsis, and epiphaneia, all denoting the visible bodily coming. That single return-vocabulary supplies strong unitary footing for reading 1 Thessalonians 4 and Matthew 24 as one event after the tribulation, and Matthew's meta makes the sequence explicit. Three lexical realities keep the question contested. First, the verb for being caught up, harpazo, is used in the canon both for sudden divine rescue (Philip in Acts 8, Paul in 2 Corinthians 12, the child in Revelation 12) and for forcible seizure, and it carries no temporal marker about when relative to the tribulation. Second, Revelation 3:10, tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou, uses the exact same construction (tereo plus ek) as John 17:15, where Jesus explicitly prays not for removal but for preservation while in. The same words have opposite spatial force in their two canon attestations. Third, ekklesia appears twenty times in Revelation but only in chapters 1 to 3 and at 22:16, with no occurrences in chapters 4 to 19. One reader sees a removal in that silence; another notes that hagioi and eklektoi vocabulary continues throughout, and Revelation 20:4 describes saints who refused the beast and his mark, which by lexicon means they were on earth during that era. Because the canon's words are agreed but the sequencing model is supplied by synthesis, the proposition lands as genuinely disputed.
